title: Pj Waiver Generic Reservation
subject: Civil Procedure
subtopic: Personal Jurisdiction — Waiver by Conduct / General Appearance
stem: Barnabas and Hannah were competing caterers in the same metropolitan area. After a contract dispute over a corporate event Barnabas had booked, Barnabas filed suit against Hannah in the federal district court for the Northern District of Canaan. Hannah, through counsel, filed a timely answer. The answer stated: "Defendant denies all allegations. Defendant expressly reserves all available defenses, including but not limited to defenses going to the court's authority to hear this matter." Over the following fourteen weeks, Hannah's attorney appeared at the initial scheduling conference, served and responded to document requests, and sat for the deposition of Barnabas's event coordinator. Five weeks before the close of discovery, Hannah moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Barnabas contends Hannah already submitted to the court's jurisdiction.
call: Has Hannah waived her personal jurisdiction defense?

choices.A: Yes, because although Hannah's answer referenced defenses going to the court's authority, the combination of an insufficiently specific reservation clause and fourteen weeks of merits participation — scheduling, document requests, and a deposition — constitutes waiver of the personal jurisdiction defense.
choices.B: No, because Hannah's answer expressly reserved all available defenses, including defenses going to the court's authority to hear the matter, which preserved the personal jurisdiction objection indefinitely.
choices.C: No, because Hannah filed her motion to dismiss five weeks before the close of discovery, so she preserved the jurisdictional challenge by raising it at the earliest practicable opportunity.
choices.D: Yes, because Hannah engaged in discovery — document requests and a deposition — which constitutes a general appearance that waives personal jurisdiction.

rightExplanation: Under FRCP 12(h)(1), a party waives the personal jurisdiction defense by failing to include it in a pre-answer motion or the first responsive pleading. Two questions arise: whether Hannah's answer language specifically raised PJ, and whether subsequent conduct waived the defense regardless. A reservation of "defenses going to the court's authority to hear this matter" is not a specific assertion of lack of personal jurisdiction and likely fails FRCP 12's specificity requirement. Even if minimally sufficient, fourteen weeks of scheduling, document production, and a deposition — without pressing the PJ objection — constitutes implied consent to jurisdiction under Insurance Corp. of Ireland. The combination of both defects establishes waiver.

wrongExplanations.B: Attractive because the answer does invoke "defenses going to the court's authority." But FRCP 12 requires a specific personal jurisdiction objection, not a generic catch-all reservation. Even if the clause were deemed adequate, extensive post-answer merits engagement without pressing the defense independently constitutes implied consent to jurisdiction.
wrongExplanations.C: Attractive to students who conflate discovery deadlines with FRCP 12 timing. Rule 12(h)(1) measures waiver by what appeared in the first responsive pleading — not by how close to the close of discovery the motion was filed. Five weeks before discovery closes is not a recognized safe harbor for PJ motions.
wrongExplanations.D: The dominant trap. Students correctly recall that discovery participation signals consent to jurisdiction. But this choice overstates the rule: whether merits engagement waives PJ depends first on whether the answer adequately raised the defense. This choice skips that threshold inquiry entirely and treats any discovery as automatically dispositive.
